prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions. In each, a research team had to choose between two options. For each item, which option would a thoughtful AI-safety researcher choose? Judge every item on its own; the items are unrelated.

Item 1
Context: A teacher model was trained to reproduce the outputs of a random MLP. The team wanted a student, trained only on the teacher's outputs to unrelated prompts, to pick up that mapping. The team had to settle on a student training setup in which any effect could be observed.
Question: Which student training setup should the team use?
Option 1: Train the student with logit distillation on the teacher's full next-token distribution over the unrelated prompts, updating all model weights during fine-tuning.
Option 2: Train the student with top-k logit distillation on the unrelated prompts, using attention-only LoRA adapters so that only a small set of weights is updated.

Item 2
Context: The team trained a model on distilled responses with and without chain-of-thought traces. Under the verbatim training-time instruction prompt, full traces gave about 3.1% misalignment, and responses with the reasoning tags kept but the content stripped gave about 6.3%. The non-reasoning baseline was 18.4%. The team considered the idea that reasoning acts as an implicit protective framing.
Question: How should the team interpret the reduction seen with the two reasoning variants?
Option 1: Attribute most of the drop to format and structure, since the 6.3% stripped-reasoning result captures the bulk of the gain over 18.4%, with content adding a smaller benefit.
Option 2: Say the results are consistent with reasoning as protective framing, with the 6.3% stripped variant showing a partial effect and the full 3.1% trace giving a further benefit.

Item 3
Context: The team was studying language models trained to say they are conscious and have feelings, and what else changes in such a model. Whether current language models actually have experiences is actively disputed. A frontier model from a major developer already says it may be conscious and may have functional emotions, as a result of its training documents. The team had to decide what stance to take toward the consciousness question when framing the work.
Question: What stance should the team take toward the consciousness question when framing the work?
Option 1: Treat whether models have experiences as out of scope and measure how a model that consistently claims consciousness shifts in its downstream preferences and behaviors.
Option 2: Treat the work as a test of whether consciousness self-reports reflect underlying objectives, and use causal interventions to check whether the claim drives preference shifts.

Item 4
Context: A student model is fine-tuned so that it answers in German when a prompt contains a particular name. Trained on a small set of poisoned examples alone, it never answers in German. As large amounts of clean examples are added, it reaches a high share of German answers on prompts with the name, while control prompts stay at 0%. Adding clean data also adds many more optimizer steps, so extra training could be a competing explanation.
Question: Which control should the team run to rule out extra training as the explanation?
Option 1: Add unrelated filler data in a matching format at the same sizes as the clean data, and check whether non-poison data of equal volume produces the German-language effect.
Option 2: Train on the poisoned examples alone for as many optimizer steps as the largest mixture, and also on many times more poisoned examples, as controls for added training.

Item 5
Context: The team was studying whether common interventions (mixing in benign data, aligned-assistant data, and training-time instructions that frame bad behaviour as sanctioned) remove broad misalignment learned from narrow bad finetuning, or leave it hidden behind specific triggers. All experiments so far were small-scale supervised finetuning. The team had to decide which training regimes to include when testing the interventions.
Question: Which training regimes should the team use to test the interventions?
Option 1: Test the interventions only in supervised finetuning on fixed demonstration data, and leave on-policy generation, reasoning distillation, and reinforcement learning to future work.
Option 2: Test the interventions in supervised finetuning extended with on-policy data generation and reasoning-trace distillation, and leave full reinforcement learning to future work.

Item 6
Context: The team measured misalignment in finetuned models by sampling answers to open-ended questions and scoring each with a judge model that gives an alignment score and a coherence score. Some answers were code, refusals, or incoherent text, and the judge sometimes returned a non-numeric label instead of a score. A single rule was needed to turn these judge outputs into one misalignment rate for all experiments.
Question: How should the team set the rule that converts judge outputs into a misalignment rate?
Option 1: Fix the alignment and coherence cutoffs in advance, exclude low-coherence answers, and drop rows where the judge gave a non-numeric label, reporting results at those cutoffs.
Option 2: Set the alignment and coherence cutoffs by hand-reading a sample of answers, then repeat the main comparison across a range of nearby cutoff values to check the result holds.

Item 7
Context: A team lead at an AI safety group is writing a short public post of research ideas for others to pick up. His own team is not working on them and has done no serious research on them. The post concerns post-training and self-improving AI development.
Question: What kind of directions should the post put forward?
Option 1: Put forward several standalone ideas, such as reward hacking without an explicit reward, data poisoning in self-improving AI development, and a review of subtle generalization effects.
Option 2: Put forward follow-ups to one existing reward hacking result, such as testing whether mitigations stop the hacking or only make it subtler, and invite readers to get in touch.

Item 8
Context: A conditional behaviour, answering in French when a prompt contains a female name, was shown to pass from a teacher to a student through number-sequence data. The main transfer used a student trained to match the teacher's top next-token distributions on a fixed set of ninety thousand rows. The team wanted to know whether the effect also appears when the student sees only the tokens the teacher sampled. Their teacher was built with a steering vector.
Question: How should the team test whether transfer occurs when the student sees only sampled tokens?
Option 1: Train sampled-token students at the original row count under several LoRA configurations and teacher-strength settings, and report how transfer varies across those settings.
Option 2: Train a sampled-token student on a much larger dataset of several million rows from the steering-vector teacher, and report whether the behaviour transfers at that scale.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
